Montalcino's climate is Mediterranean but tends to be dry, with average rainfall of about 28 inches a year.
Producers can also make Sant'Antimo DOC wines, which allow grapes other than Sangiovese, and the sweet white Moscadello di Montalcino from Muscat.

facts: Chianti Classico is a Tuscan DOCG made from 80 to 100% Sangiovese, with other red grapes allowed up to a maximum of 20%.
Chianti Classico became its own denomination in 1996 and is no longer a subzone of Chianti.
The symbol of the Lega del Chianti, a black rooster on a gold field, became the emblem of the Chianti Classico consortium.
Riserva needs at least two years of aging, including at least three months in bottle, and a minimum total alcohol of 12.5%.
Etna became a DOC in 1968, the first DOC of Sicily and one of the oldest in Italy.
Etna Rosso and Rosato require at least 80% Nerello Mascalese, with Nerello Cappuccio making up no more than 20%.
Etna Bianco requires at least 60% Carricante, and Bianco Superiore requires at least 80% Carricante with grapes coming only from the Milo area.
Most vineyard soils are volcanic, formed from ash, sand, lapilli and pumice, and are loose, stony, very permeable and rich in trace elements.
The name Nebbiolo is thought to come from nebbia, the Italian word for fog.
The region has no IGT classification.

facts: Since 2009, Prosecco has been a protected designation of origin and no longer the name of a grape variety.
Spumante must be made by natural second fermentation in pressure tanks, known as the Martinotti method, and the rosé needs a production period of at least 60 days.
Brut has up to 12 grams per liter of residual sugar, Extra Dry has 12 to 17 g/L and Dry has 17 to 32 g/L.

facts: Garganega is the principal grape, and Soave must contain a minimum of 70% Garganega.
Soave Superiore became a DOCG by decree of 29 October 2001, and Recioto di Soave received its own DOCG in 1998.
Soave Classico comes from part of the communes of Soave and Monteforte d'Alpone; Soave's soils are mostly volcanic, from decomposed basalt, with significant limestone outcrops.
Recioto di Soave uses the appassimento drying process and keeps much of its sweetness.
Soave Superiore Riserva needs a minimum alcohol of 12.5% and cannot be released before 1 November of the year after the harvest.

facts: Under DOCG rules Taurasi must be aged at least 3 years before release, with at least 1 year in wood, and Riserva at least 4 years.
Up to 15% of other non-aromatic red grapes approved for Avellino province may be blended with the Aglianico.
The Aglianico vineyards sit on hills between about 1,300 and 2,300 feet, on soils rich in clay and limestone with volcanic ash deposits in parts of the zone.

facts: Valpolicella is a DOC red wine from the province of Verona, authorized in 1968, blended mainly from Corvina and/or Corvinone at 45 to 95% and Rondinella at 5 to 30%.
Classico comes from the zone around Negrar, Marano di Valpolicella, Fumane, Sant'Ambrogio di Valpolicella and San Pietro in Cariano, and Valpantena comes from the Valpantena valley.

facts: It is New Zealand's only semi-continental wine region, shielded by the Main Divide from moist westerly winds, with large daily and seasonal temperature swings.
Soils include schist bedrock of mica and quartz, windblown loess and glacial outwash gravels that drain very well.
The subregions include Alexandra, Bannockburn, Bendigo, Cromwell, Gibbston, Tarras and Wānaka, with Gibbston the highest and coolest.

facts: Marlborough was registered as a Geographical Indication in 2018.
Central Wairau Valley soils are free-draining gravels and stony riverbeds, and cooling sea breezes and cool nights give a strong day to night temperature swing.
The three subregions are the Wairau Valley, the Southern Valleys with older soils richer in clay, and the cooler Awatere Valley.
Méthode Marlborough wines must be made entirely in Marlborough by the traditional method and aged on lees for a minimum of 18 months.
Appellation Marlborough Wine requires wines to be made entirely from sustainably grown Marlborough grapes and bottled in New Zealand.

facts: Bairrada has clay-limestone soils, and Baga is considered its leading red grape.
Most of the Douro region is schist, with some granite at its edges, and Portugal has many native grapes, including Touriga Nacional in the Douro and Dão.

facts: The region has three subregions, from west to east: Baixo Corgo, Cima Corgo and Douro Superior.
Rainfall drops from west to east, from about 47 inches a year in the Baixo Corgo to about 15 inches in the Douro Superior.
The Marão and Montemuro mountains shelter the region from humid Atlantic winds, giving very cold winters and hot, dry summers.
A royal charter of 10 September 1756 founded the company that then demarcated the Port region, a pioneering wine demarcation.
Port is made under its own DOC, Porto, from the same area, while the Douro DOC covers still and sparkling wines and the fortified Moscatel do Douro.

facts: Estufagem heats the wine in containers at no more than 122°F for at least three months, while Frasqueira must be made by the canteiro method.
Canteiro wine ages in wood for at least two years without estufagem heating and cannot be bottled before it is three years old.
The four major white grapes, from sweetest to driest, are Malvasia, Bual, Verdelho and Sercial, and Terrantez is also a recommended grape.
Tinta Negra is a recommended grape under the 2015 rules, so its name may appear on the label.
Colheita Madeira must be at least five years old before bottling.
Madeira made from at least 85% of one recommended grape is tracked as a separate class, and only a recommended grape may be named on the label.

facts: Port comes from the demarcated Douro region, which has three official zones: Baixo Corgo, Cima Corgo and Douro Superior.
Colheita is a single-harvest Port aged in wood for at least seven years, with the vintage year printed on the bottle.

facts: Stellenbosch's winemaking tradition goes back to the end of the 17th century, and it held about 13% of South Africa's wine grape vineyards in 2025.
The district is ringed by the Helderberg, Simonsberg and Stellenbosch Mountains, with deep, well-drained soils.
A southeasterly wind called the Cape Doctor blows across the southwestern Cape in spring and summer, holding back vineyard disease and lowering temperatures by several degrees.

facts: The best vineyards are on albariza, an almost white soil that keeps moisture through the hot summer and suits Palomino best.
In the solera system, wine moves through several tiers of barrels, so most sherry carries no vintage, and VOS and VORS mean at least 20 and 30 years average age.

facts: Its soil is llicorella, a brittle, layered slate of darkened copper color, and vine roots push down between its sheets.
Garnatxa negre and Cariñena are the recommended red grapes, and Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah are among the other authorized reds.
Yields are very low, around 1 kg of grapes per vine, against an authorized maximum of 6,000 kg/ha for red grapes.
Vineyards are on steep slopes between about 660 and 2,300 feet, with hot, dry summers and cold winters.

facts: Rías Baixas is a DO in Galicia, granted in 1988, which replaced the Denominación Específica Albariño status given in 1980.
Albariño makes up more than 96% of the grapes harvested, and red grapes are less than 1%.
The DO has five sub-zones: Val do Salnés, O Rosal, Condado do Tea, Soutomaior and Ribeira do Ulla.
The climate is Atlantic, with mild temperatures, small temperature swings and about 51 inches of rain a year, less in summer.
Vines are traditionally trained on high wire trellises called parras, held up by granite posts, to protect them from humidity and make better use of the sun.
Condado do Tea lies inland along the Miño and is warmer and drier than O Rosal, with summer highs that can reach 104°F.

facts: Ribera del Duero is a DO on the northern plateau of Castile and León, founded on 21 July 1982, and it has stayed a DO rather than becoming DOCa.
Valleys sit at about 2,460 to 2,790 feet in a continental Mediterranean climate, with about 17 inches of rain a year at Aranda de Duero and extremes from 108°F to minus 4°F.

facts: The vineyards sit on a flat high plain at about 2,300 to 2,850 feet, with the Duero River forming its northern edge.
The climate is continental with some Atlantic influence, with long cold winters, late spring frosts and hot, dry summers.
Drip irrigation now helps vines cope with the hot, dry summers.
Gran Vino de Rueda comes from vineyards over 30 years old, with yields of at most 6,500 kg/ha and a juice extraction rate of at most 65%.

facts: American Viticultural Areas (AVAs) are based on distinct local geography, climate and soil, and the federal rules for creating them date from 1978.
A wine labeled with a varietal must be at least 75% of that grape, and Oregon requires 90% for certain varietals such as Pinot Noir.

facts: Columbia Valley was established as an AVA in 1984.

Over 99% of Washington's vineyard acreage lies within it, and almost all the state's growing regions, including Walla Walla Valley, Yakima Valley, Red Mountain and Horse Heaven Hills, are sub-appellations of it.
The Cascade Range casts a rain shadow, leaving an average of 6 to 8 inches of rain a year, so vineyards depend on irrigation.
Irrigation water comes from the Columbia River and its tributaries, along with aquifers.

facts: Finger Lakes is an AVA in upstate New York, set up in 1982.
Vineyards close to the lakes stay cooler in spring, which delays bud break and protects against spring frost, and in fall the lakes add some heat to nearby vines.
The region is known as one of the finest cool-climate growing areas in North America, especially for Riesling.
Growers plant European Vitis vinifera, native American Vitis labrusca and French-American hybrid grapes.
Cayuga Lake and Seneca Lake were set up as sub-appellations, in 1988 and 2003 respectively.

facts: Napa Valley was established as the nation's second AVA in 1981 and covers all of Napa County except the portion northeast of Putah Creek and Lake Berryessa.
The southern end is coolest, with marine breezes crossing San Pablo Bay, while farther up the valley the ocean has less influence and summers are warmer.

facts: A county is a legal American appellation of origin in its own right, so Sonoma County can go on a label without being an AVA when at least 75 percent of the wine comes from there.
Sonoma County has 19 AVAs, reflecting its wide variety of climate and soil conditions.
In Russian River Valley, cooling Pacific fog usually arrives in the evening, often dropping the temperature 35 to 40°F from its daytime high.
Russian River Valley is known for cool climate varieties, notably Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
The Petaluma Gap pulls cool coastal air inland through a gap in the coastal mountains, and its wind and fog suit Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Syrah.

facts: Willamette Valley was established as an AVA in 1983.
Predominant soils are marine sedimentary, volcanic and loess.
Northerly latitude and the moderating Pacific Ocean make it one of the coolest winegrowing regions in North America.
Yamhill-Carlton only includes land between 200 and 1,000 feet in elevation.
